action: Replace fragment lists with actual sentences; deletion test — if nothing is lost besides rhythm, the fragments are decoration
notes: Source bounds: 'One of these per chapter is a stylistic choice. Twenty-five per chapter is a nervous breakdown formatted as literature.' Threshold 5 is a harness-derived midpoint — clearly above the stylistic-choice bound (1), far below the breakdown bound (25); harness-default threshold. Best-effort regex = 3+ consecutive sentences of <=4 words; verbless/fragment status needs judgment confirm. engine:consecutive. Examples: 'Bodies. Thousands of them.' 'Heroes. Liberators. Gratitude.'

action: Reserve for genuine turns; if every fourth paragraph is a single solemn sentence, no moment matters because all moments matter equally
notes: Source: 'Reserve these for genuine turns. If you have more than two per scene, you're scoring a film, not writing a story.' → max 2 per scene. engine:para-one-sentence (counts paragraphs consisting of exactly one sentence, <=25 words; dialogue-bearing paragraphs excluded — a tagged spoken line is normal speech, not a gravity beat). Examples: 'No one spoke.' 'The room fell silent.' 'That was deliberate.'

action: Delete the echo; if the first sentence isn't strong enough to stand alone, replace it — don't prop it up with a backup singer
notes: Test verbatim: 'does the second sentence contain any information not already in the first? If the answer is no, you've been amplified.' engine:consecutive (adjacent sentence pair). Regex is a best-effort signature for the negation+echo form ('He did not hurry. He never did.' / 'It did not work on him. Very little did.'); the general restate-it-harder echo is judgment-confirmed.

regex: \b(?:silence settled(?: over the \w+)?|no one spoke|the \w+ fell silent|a long silence followed)\b
action: Cut — if the statement is strong, the silence is implied; show who breaks the silence, who endures it, what it costs
notes: Source: 'If you have more than two per scene, your characters are spending more time not talking than talking.' → CAP 2 per scene, counting the listed phrases collectively (alternation). Complete source phrase list: 'Silence settled over the room.' 'No one spoke.' 'The room fell silent.' 'A long silence followed.' ('room' mildly generalized to any noun). 'AI uses silence as a transition the way bad PowerPoints use fade-to-black.'

action: Vary — sometimes one smell is enough, sometimes a room doesn't smell like anything worth mentioning; sometimes the important sensory detail is a sound, a texture, or the cold
notes: Source: 'Every room your character enters gets exactly three smells.' engine:per-paragraph (flag paragraphs enumerating smell triads; escalate when smells are described in three consecutive rooms — 'your prose has a sinus infection'). Best-effort regex needs a smell/scent keyword; keyword-free scent triads ('Therra blossom, ironroot, and mint') need judgment.

action: Use plain language for plain sensory facts ('faint smell of fish skin'); save the poetry for when it does real work
source_ref: collation:1239-1245 [reddit10 field guide item 3]; collation:1232 [item 2 examples]
notes: Source examples (complete): 'a ghost of smoked fish skin', 'a whisper of aged leather', 'a memory of burnt cedar', plus 'a trace of salt wind' from item 2. WATCH not BANNED because source explicitly permits poetry 'when it does real work'. 'Abstract noun + sensory detail = sounds poetic, means nothing.' Caveat: literal uses ('a memory of his father surfaced') are not violations — flag only when decorating sensory detail.

regex: (?:,|\.)\s*which was (?:another way of saying|a generous \w+ for|either)\b|\beither [^.!?]{1,50} or [^.!?]{1,50} depending on\b
action: Apply the deletion test: if the trailing clause contains a fact, keep it; if it contains only tone, cut it
notes: Source: 'One of these per page is a voice. Five per page is a tic.' Harness-derived per-chapter cap of 4 (conservative mapping of the page-based bounds onto the chapter unit; harness-default threshold — a strict 1/page voice level would allow far more per chapter). Special mention verbatim: the 'which was either X or Y depending on Z' construction 'sounds thoughtful without committing to either one'. Regex catches signature forms only; general trailing-irony clauses need judgment.

action: Pick one or two items that reveal character or world; summarize the rest — nobody needs the receipt
notes: engine:per-paragraph. Applies to market purchases with running arithmetic ('One and a half silver gone, just like that'), gear checks ('Bow strung. Quiver full. Knife secure. Pack ready.'), base tours ('They passed the gym. Then the laundromat. Then the formation area.'), and ship descriptions (one paragraph per subsystem). Best-effort: 5+ consecutive ultra-short sentences or repeated 'Then the X.' — enumeration intent needs judgment confirm.

action: Cover the stage direction with your hand; read the dialogue alone — if the emotion is obvious, the stage direction is a subtitle; cut it
notes: Source examples: Her hands trembled. 'Please don't go.' / His jaw clenched, anger rising in his chest. 'I said no.' / A wave of grief washed over her. 'She's gone, isn't she.' / His voice was barely a whisper. 'Do you still love me?' 'It's the prose equivalent of a laugh track.' Best-effort adjacency heuristic (dialogue + body-reaction keyword on the same line, either order); redundancy itself is judgment — a body beat that ADDS information is fine.

action: Show the reader through action, dialogue, or a specific observed detail; or say it plainly ('she was compelling') and move on
notes: Noun list taken verbatim from source examples: 'They were memory, flaw, hunger.' 'She was silence, patience, and rage.' 'He was ambition in a green hood.' 'It asserts depth without demonstrating it' — the character-description equivalent of a motivational poster. Other abstract nouns in the same frame need judgment.

action: Justify or cut — these are things to justify, not default sentence starters; cohere through reference and sentence shape instead
notes: Complete opener list from source: Furthermore, Moreover, Additionally, Importantly, Notably. Not BANNED — safety rails protect 'however' and competent connectives; justified uses exist. Cluster row: report counts; tripwire from check 5 applies (same move 3+ times or dominating two consecutive paragraphs → rewrite one).

regex: \b(?:it depends|on the one hand|here['’]?s a nuanced take)\b|\bperhaps\b[^.!?]{0,80}\bperhaps\b|\bI think\b[^.!?]{0,40}\b(?:maybe|sort of)\b
action: Commit to a sharp emotional or sensory choice; cut the hedge tax where a cleaner sentence would do
source_ref: collation:81 [catalog of quirks: hedging]; collation:3112 [Writing ruleset formula list]
notes: Catalog phrases (complete): 'it depends', 'on the one hand', 'perhaps', 'here's a nuanced take'. Ruleset adds fake-human hedge chains ('I think... maybe... sort of') flagged only 'when the uncertainty is not real'. A single 'perhaps' is NOT flagged; regex catches perhaps-stacking within a sentence. Source caveat: in fiction the equivalent is 'a narratorial reluctance to commit to a sharp emotional or sensory choice' — judgment territory.

action: Break the repeated pattern where it starts to dominate; rewrite at least one occurrence when the move appears 3+ times or dominates two consecutive paragraphs
notes: Safety rail: single use is legitimate — 'the recurring problem is regularity and mismatch, not any one feature'; never BANNED. Forms from source: 'not X, but Y'; 'may sound X, but Y'; 'It's not X, it's Y'; 'This is not just..., it is...'. Em-dash variants ('not X — Y') counted by judgment.

action: Replace the type-definition closer with a concrete consequence, or cut
notes: Source form: paragraph-closing type definitions ('the kind of X where Y'). engine:per-paragraph — weight matches landing in a paragraph's final sentence; mid-paragraph use is a weaker signal. 'sort/type' added as obvious surface variants of the same move.

action: Rewrite at least one occurrence around a single consequence, contrast, or example when list work dominates
source_ref: collation:2950-2962 [Writing ruleset rule 10]; collation:3110 [formula list]; collation:3068 [hidden-list audit]
notes: Source: 'parallel enumeration and reflexive three-part cadence inside sentences'; 'Three-item parallel lists still count. Changing X, Y, Z, and W to X, Y, and Z does not fix the underlying shape.' High-noise counter — legitimate lists also match; report density only and NEVER block (safety rails: well-formed prose may not be BANNED). Doubles as a partial greppable proxy for hidden list work (hidden-list audit: 3+ sentences doing list work → rewrite one); full hidden-list detection is judgment.

action: Vary your word choices — do not repeat the same descriptor twice in a scene
notes: engine:repeated-descriptor — the engine tracks descriptor/adjective reuse within scene boundaries; not expressible as a line regex, so the regex field is the __ENGINE__ placeholder. Source rule verbatim: 'Don't repeat the same descriptor twice in a scene.' Source also names overused AI favorites to avoid: mused, whispered, crimson, azure, ethereal ('It's not that they're bad words - they just get stale').
